purpose: Approved Marrow ED8 Biochemistry Chapter 9 explanation rollout. Raw imported source remains immutable; this file contains learner-facing augmentation only.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q001.takeaway: Musty odor plus a positive Guthrie test indicates phenylketonuria; tryptophan deficiency is not a feature.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q001.displayText:
The presentation is classic for phenylketonuria (PKU), usually caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency. Phenylalanine and alternative metabolites such as phenylpyruvate and phenylacetate accumulate.

PKU causes neurodevelopmental impairment and hypopigmentation because less phenylalanine is converted to tyrosine, reducing melanin synthesis. A white patch of hair due to tryptophan deficiency is not a characteristic feature.

rationales.a: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency is the classic enzyme defect in PKU and is therefore a true statement.
rationales.c: Phenylacetate is one of the alternative phenylalanine metabolites that can be excreted in PKU.
rationales.d: Untreated PKU can cause severe intellectual and developmental impairment, so this is a true feature.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q002.takeaway: The ferric-chloride urine test in PKU detects phenylpyruvate.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q002.displayText:
Elevated phenylalanine with developmental delay and seizures suggests phenylketonuria. In the ferric chloride test, urinary phenylpyruvate reacts to produce a transient green color.

Phenylpyruvate is formed through an alternative pathway of phenylalanine metabolism when the normal phenylalanine-to-tyrosine route is impaired.

rationales.a: Phenylacetate may occur in PKU but is not the metabolite detected by the source-keyed ferric-chloride test.
rationales.b: Phenyllactate is an alternative phenylalanine metabolite but is not the source-keyed FeCl3-positive analyte.
rationales.d: Phenylalanine itself is elevated in blood but is not what the urine ferric-chloride test is detecting here.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q003.takeaway: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes type I tyrosinemia.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q003.displayText:
Type I tyrosinemia, also called hepatorenal tyrosinemia, is caused by deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase in tyrosine degradation.

The source contrasts this with type II tyrosinemia from tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency and neonatal/type III tyrosinemia from a different downstream defect.

rationales.b: Type II tyrosinemia is associated with tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency, not fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency.
rationales.c: The source associates neonatal/type III tyrosinemia with a different enzyme defect.
rationales.d: Type IV is not the source-keyed disorder caused by fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q004.takeaway: Type I tyrosinemia is treated with nitisinone plus dietary restriction of tyrosine and phenylalanine.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q004.displayText:
Jaundice, hepatomegaly, boiled-cabbage odor and elevated succinylacetone indicate type I tyrosinemia. Treatment combines nitisinone (NTBC) with dietary restriction of tyrosine and phenylalanine.

Nitisinone blocks an upstream step in tyrosine degradation and reduces formation of toxic downstream metabolites. Because all three listed measures are part of treatment, “All of the above” is correct.

rationales.a: Phenylalanine restriction is part of dietary management because phenylalanine can be converted to tyrosine.
rationales.b: Tyrosine restriction directly reduces substrate entering the defective degradation pathway.
rationales.c: Nitisinone is a key drug used to reduce formation of toxic metabolites in type I tyrosinemia.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q005.takeaway: Richner–Hanhart syndrome is type II tyrosinemia caused by tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q005.displayText:
Richner–Hanhart syndrome is oculocutaneous tyrosinemia, or type II tyrosinemia. It is caused by deficiency of tyrosine aminotransferase.

The source notes painful palmoplantar hyperkeratotic lesions and ocular involvement as characteristic manifestations.

rationales.a: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes type I tyrosinemia.
rationales.c: The source associates 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate-pathway deficiency with neonatal/type III tyrosinemia rather than Richner–Hanhart syndrome.
rationales.d: Homogentisate oxidase deficiency causes alkaptonuria.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q006.takeaway: The source attributes neonatal tyrosinemia to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase deficiency.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q006.displayText:
Neonatal tyrosinemia is source-keyed to deficiency of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase in the tyrosine-degradation pathway.

The source contrasts type I tyrosinemia with fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency and type II with tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency.

rationales.a: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes type I hepatorenal tyrosinemia.
rationales.b: Tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency causes type II oculocutaneous tyrosinemia.
rationales.c: Tyrosinase deficiency causes albinism rather than neonatal tyrosinemia.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q007.takeaway: Classic oculocutaneous albinism is caused by deficient tyrosinase activity.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q007.displayText:
The image is source-interpreted as albinism, with very pale skin and white hair. The classic biochemical defect is deficient activity of tyrosinase, a copper-containing enzyme required for melanin synthesis from tyrosine-derived intermediates.

The source image remains preserved separately.

rationales.b: Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis, not melanin formation.
rationales.c: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes PKU; hypopigmentation can occur but does not match the severe albinism image as well.
rationales.d: Tyrosine transaminase deficiency causes type II tyrosinemia, not classic albinism.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q008.takeaway: Urine that turns black on standing plus ochronosis is characteristic of alkaptonuria.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q008.displayText:
Blackening of urine on standing and bluish-black pigmentation of the sclera or pinna indicate alkaptonuria. The disorder results from homogentisate oxidase deficiency, causing homogentisic acid accumulation.

Oxidation and polymerization of homogentisic acid produce dark pigment that deposits in connective tissue, a process called ochronosis. The source image remains preserved separately.

rationales.a: Phenylketonuria causes phenylalanine accumulation and neurodevelopmental features, not black urine on standing with ochronosis.
rationales.c: Tyrosinemia causes different tyrosine-catabolic defects and does not produce the classic ochronotic black-urine pattern.
rationales.d: Maple-syrup urine disease produces a sweet burnt-sugar odor rather than urine that blackens on standing.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q009.takeaway: Ochronotic pigmentation with calcified intervertebral discs points to alkaptonuria.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q009.displayText:
Blackish connective-tissue pigmentation together with progressive back stiffness and calcification of intervertebral discs is classic for ochronotic spondyloarthropathy in alkaptonuria.

Homogentisate oxidase deficiency causes homogentisic acid accumulation, black urine on standing and pigment deposition in cartilage and collagen. The source images remain preserved separately.

rationales.a: Phenylketonuria does not cause ochronotic pigmentation and intervertebral-disc calcification.
rationales.c: Maple-syrup urine disease presents with branched-chain amino-acid toxicity, not ochronotic spondyloarthropathy.
rationales.d: Tyrosinemia does not produce the characteristic black connective-tissue pigment and disc calcification.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q010.takeaway: Hartnup disease impairs transport of tryptophan and other neutral amino acids.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q010.displayText:
Neutral aminoaciduria with pellagra-like dermatitis, diarrhea and neuropsychiatric findings suggests Hartnup disease. The defect affects renal and intestinal transport of neutral amino acids, especially tryptophan.

Because tryptophan is a precursor of niacin, impaired absorption can produce pellagra-like features. Indole metabolites can be detected by the Obermeyer test.

rationales.a: Tyrosine is neutral, but tryptophan is the key source amino acid linked to the niacin-deficiency manifestations of Hartnup disease.
rationales.c: Phenylalanine is also neutral, but the source-keyed amino acid explaining the pellagra-like syndrome is tryptophan.
rationales.d: Threonine is neutral but is not the principal source-keyed amino acid associated with the classic Hartnup presentation.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q011.takeaway: Vitamin B6 deficiency can cause xanthurenic aciduria by impairing kynureninase.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q011.displayText:
During tryptophan metabolism, kynureninase requires pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6. Deficiency of vitamin B6 impairs this step and promotes formation and urinary excretion of xanthurenic acid.

Thus xanthurenic aciduria is a marker of impaired B6-dependent tryptophan metabolism.

rationales.a: Vitamin B2 is not the source-keyed deficiency causing xanthurenic acid accumulation in this pathway.
rationales.b: Vitamin B3 is niacin itself; its deficiency does not directly produce the source-keyed kynureninase block.
rationales.c: Vitamin B5 is not the PLP source required by kynureninase.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q012.takeaway: Excess urinary 5-HIAA is a classic biochemical marker of carcinoid syndrome.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q012.displayText:
Carcinoid tumors can overproduce serotonin, producing flushing, bronchospasm, abdominal cramps and diarrhea. Serotonin is metabolized to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), which is excreted in urine.

Therefore excessive urinary 5-HIAA supports carcinoid syndrome.

rationales.a: Alkaptonuria is associated with homogentisic acid, not 5-HIAA.
rationales.b: Albinism reflects impaired melanin synthesis and does not cause excess urinary 5-HIAA.
rationales.d: Phenylketonuria produces alternative phenylalanine metabolites rather than excessive serotonin-derived 5-HIAA.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q013.takeaway: Cystinuria causes urinary loss of cystine plus COLA amino acids; histidine is not part of the defect.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q013.displayText:
Hexagonal urinary crystals indicate cystinuria. The renal and intestinal transport defect affects cystine and the dibasic amino acids Ornithine, Lysine and Arginine—the COLA mnemonic.

Histidine is not part of this transporter defect. The source image remains preserved separately.

rationales.a: Ornithine is one of the dibasic amino acids lost in cystinuria.
rationales.b: Lysine is included in the COLA group transported abnormally in cystinuria.
rationales.c: Arginine is also one of the dibasic amino acids affected in cystinuria.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q014.takeaway: Disordered sulfur-amino-acid metabolism can raise homocysteine and cardiovascular risk.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q014.displayText:
Cystathionine β-synthase deficiency causes homocystinuria, a disorder of sulfur-containing amino-acid metabolism. Homocysteine accumulation is associated with endothelial injury and a strong tendency toward thrombosis.

That thrombotic risk explains the increased cardiovascular risk linked to defective sulfur-amino-acid metabolism.

rationales.a: Branched-chain amino-acid defects cause disorders such as MSUD but are not the source-keyed cause of homocysteine-associated cardiovascular risk.
rationales.b: Aromatic amino-acid disorders include PKU and tyrosinemias, not the homocysteine-thrombosis pathway asked here.
rationales.d: Imino-acid metabolism is not the source-linked pathway responsible for elevated homocysteine and vascular risk.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q015.takeaway: Downward lens subluxation, marfanoid habitus and pediatric thrombosis indicate homocystinuria.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q015.displayText:
A tall, thin child with elongated limbs, ectopia lentis and an acute thrombotic event strongly suggests homocystinuria. The common defect is cystathionine β-synthase deficiency, leading to accumulation of homocysteine and methionine.

A high-yield distinction from Marfan syndrome is lens direction: the source notes downward/nasal subluxation in homocystinuria versus upward/temporal displacement in Marfan syndrome. The source image remains preserved separately.

rationales.a: Cystinuria causes recurrent cystine stones and COLA aminoaciduria, not marfanoid habitus with ectopia lentis and thrombosis.
rationales.c: Cystinosis is a lysosomal cystine-storage disorder and does not fit this thrombotic marfanoid phenotype.
rationales.d: Alkaptonuria causes ochronosis and degenerative arthropathy rather than ectopia lentis with pediatric thrombosis.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q016.takeaway: Phenylketonuria is not part of Garrod's classic tetrad.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q016.displayText:
Garrod's classic inborn-error tetrad comprises alkaptonuria, albinism, cystinuria and pentosuria.

Phenylketonuria is an important inborn error of metabolism, but it is not one of the four disorders in Garrod's tetrad.

rationales.a: Alkaptonuria is one of the disorders included in Garrod's tetrad.
rationales.b: Cystinuria is included in the classic tetrad.
rationales.c: Pentosuria is also part of Garrod's tetrad.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q017.takeaway: Primary hyperoxaluria type I involves defective glyoxylate handling in glycine metabolism.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q017.displayText:
Primary hyperoxaluria type I is caused by deficiency of alanine:glyoxylate aminotransferase in liver peroxisomes. Glyoxylate cannot be adequately redirected and is instead converted to excess oxalate.

The source frames this as a defect in glycine metabolism, with oxalate overproduction causing recurrent stones and renal injury.

rationales.a: Threonine is not the source-keyed amino-acid metabolism defect in primary hyperoxaluria type I.
rationales.b: Serine is not the source-keyed substrate pathway responsible for the AGT defect described here.
rationales.d: Alanine participates in the enzyme name, but the source classifies the metabolic defect under glycine/glyoxylate metabolism.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q018.takeaway: The histidine-load test detects folate deficiency through increased urinary FIGLU.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q018.displayText:
Histidine catabolism produces formiminoglutamate (FIGLU). Transfer of its formimino group requires tetrahydrofolate.

When folate is deficient, FIGLU accumulates and is excreted in urine after a histidine load. The source pathway figure remains preserved separately.

rationales.a: Iron deficiency does not cause the source-keyed FIGLU accumulation after histidine loading.
rationales.c: Pyridoxine deficiency affects PLP-dependent reactions but is not what the histidine-load FIGLU test detects.
rationales.d: Vitamin B12 deficiency can impair one-carbon metabolism indirectly, but the classic source-keyed histidine-load test is for folate deficiency.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q019.displayText:
Canavan disease is an autosomal-recessive leukodystrophy caused by aspartoacylase deficiency. N-acetylaspartate accumulates and is excessively excreted in urine.

The source pathway figure remains preserved separately.

rationales.b: Oasthouse syndrome is not the disorder caused by aspartoacylase deficiency in the source.
rationales.c: Hawkinsinuria is a different amino-acid metabolic disorder and is not due to aspartoacylase deficiency.
rationales.d: Hartnup disease is a neutral amino-acid transport defect, not an aspartoacylase deficiency.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q020.takeaway: MSUD type I reflects defective oxidative decarboxylation of branched-chain α-ketoacids.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q020.displayText:
Maple-syrup urine disease type I involves the E1 decarboxylase component of the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. The affected step is oxidative decarboxylation.

Leucine, isoleucine and valine and their corresponding ketoacids accumulate, producing neurotoxicity and the characteristic burnt-sugar odor.

rationales.b: Oxidation is too nonspecific and is not the source-keyed defective reaction assigned to type I MSUD.
rationales.c: Carboxylation is not the defective step in the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex.
rationales.d: Deamination is not the E1 decarboxylation defect responsible for type I MSUD.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q021.takeaway: Type II MSUD is caused by mutation of the E2 dihydrolipoyl transacetylase component.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q021.displayText:
The branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex has E1, E2 and E3 components. The source classifies type II MSUD as mutation of the E2 component, dihydrolipoyl transacetylase.

Type I involves E1α/E1β defects, while type III involves the E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase component.

rationales.a: The α-ketoacid decarboxylase E1 component is associated with type I MSUD, not type II.
rationales.c: Dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase is the E3 component associated with type III MSUD.
rationales.d: A defined E2 enzyme is given, so 'None of the above' is incorrect.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q022.takeaway: Isovaleric aciduria is a defect of leucine catabolism.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q022.displayText:
Poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy and increased urinary isovaleric acid indicate isovaleric aciduria. The enzyme defect is isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase in leucine degradation.

A characteristic sweaty-feet odor can be present.

rationales.a: Isoleucine catabolism does not produce the source-keyed isovaleric-acid defect.
rationales.b: Valine catabolism is not the pathway blocked in isovaleric aciduria.
rationales.d: Lysine is not the source amino acid whose catabolism produces isovaleric acid in this disorder.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q023.takeaway: Gyrate atrophy from ornithine aminotransferase deficiency causes hyperornithinemia.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q023.displayText:
Progressive myopia and night blindness with gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina suggest ornithine aminotransferase deficiency.

The defect causes elevated plasma and urinary ornithine. The source notes that disease begins with visual symptoms in adolescence and can progress substantially over time.

rationales.a: Cystine elevation is not the source-keyed biochemical abnormality in gyrate atrophy.
rationales.c: Lysine is not the amino acid that accumulates from ornithine aminotransferase deficiency.
rationales.d: Alanine is not the source-keyed elevated plasma amino acid in this disorder.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q024.takeaway: Segawa syndrome is a BH4-deficient, dopamine-responsive dystonia.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q024.displayText:
Segawa syndrome is a hereditary dopamine-responsive dystonia linked to impaired tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis, classically from GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency.

BH4 is required for tyrosine hydroxylase, so dopamine synthesis falls. Symptoms often worsen during the day and improve after rest, and levodopa can produce a marked response.

rationales.b: Pantothenic acid deficiency does not cause the BH4-related dopamine-responsive dystonia described here.
rationales.c: Biotin deficiency causes carboxylase-related metabolic disease, not classic Segawa syndrome.
rationales.d: Tetrahydrofolate is a one-carbon carrier and is not the source-keyed deficient cofactor in Segawa syndrome.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q025.takeaway: A boiled-cabbage odor is a classic clue to hypermethioninemia.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q025.displayText:
Hypermethioninemia can produce a distinctive boiled-cabbage odor in breath, sweat and urine. The source attributes the odor to dimethyl sulfide, a methionine-derived metabolite.

One genetic cause is methionine adenosyltransferase deficiency, which impairs conversion of methionine to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM).

rationales.b: Isovaleric aciduria is classically associated with a sweaty-feet odor rather than boiled cabbage.
rationales.c: Multiple carboxylase deficiency can cause metabolic decompensation but is not the source-keyed boiled-cabbage odor disorder.
rationales.d: Trimethylaminuria produces a fishy odor, not a boiled-cabbage odor.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q026.takeaway: Trimethylaminuria is managed by reducing choline-rich precursors of trimethylamine.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q026.displayText:
Fish-odor syndrome is trimethylaminuria, usually caused by deficiency of FMO3, which normally converts trimethylamine (TMA) to odorless trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO).

Because choline is a dietary precursor of trimethylamine, choline-rich foods should be limited in affected patients.

rationales.a: Biotin is not the dietary precursor specifically avoided because of trimethylamine production.
rationales.c: Niacin is not a principal trimethylamine precursor in fish-odor syndrome.
rationales.d: Pantothenic acid is not the source-keyed dietary compound that should be restricted.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q027.takeaway: The source states that urinary 3-methylhistidine is decreased in Wilson disease.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q027.displayText:
Wilson disease is caused by ATP7B dysfunction, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and copper accumulation in liver, brain and eye.

For this question, the source specifically states that urinary 3-methylhistidine is decreased and contrasts it with broader amino-acid conjugation patterns in urine. This source-keyed biochemical detail is preserved without extending it beyond the supplied explanation.

rationales.a: Tyrosine is not the source-keyed urinary constituent reported as decreased in this Wilson-disease question.
rationales.b: Phosphorus is not the source-keyed decreased urinary analyte here.
rationales.c: Serine is not the source-keyed urinary amino acid singled out as decreased.

sourceNotes: The urinary 3-methylhistidine statement is source-keyed and relatively specialized. The augmentation preserves the source claim without adding an unsupported mechanism beyond the supplied explanation.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q028.takeaway: Black urine on standing indicates alkaptonuria from homogentisate oxidase deficiency.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH09_Q028.displayText:
Urine that turns black after exposure to air is characteristic of alkaptonuria. Homogentisate oxidase normally converts homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate in tyrosine degradation.

Deficiency causes homogentisic acid accumulation and urinary excretion; oxidation on standing darkens the urine. Chronic deposition of oxidized pigment can produce ochronosis and arthritis.

rationales.b: Xanthine oxidase deficiency causes xanthinuria and low uric acid, not black urine on standing.
rationales.c: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes phenylketonuria, not the homogentisate-associated black-urine phenotype.
rationales.d: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase defects are unrelated to the source-keyed alkaptonuria presentation.
